paper_design_summary: Narrative review that synthesizes work from linguistics, psychology, cognitive science, and computer science on how LLMs homogenize language, perspective, and reasoning. It reports no participants or data of its own, no search strategy or inclusion criteria, and no pooled estimates. Its evidence on creativity sits in one paragraph of the Reasoning Diversity section (p. 15), which cites experiments on LLM-assisted ideation (refs 124 and 125: Anderson, Shah, and Kreminski 2024; Doshi and Hauser 2024) and related work (refs 126-128).

studies.label: Narrative review of LLM homogenization of language, perspective, and reasoning (no new data)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing. The paper reviews published work and collects no data.
assignment.quote: We synthesize evidence across linguistics, psychology, cognitive science, and computer science to show how LLMs reflect and reinforce dominant styles while marginalizing alternative voices and reasoning strategies.

participants.who: No participant sample is analyzed in this narrative review; empirical findings are attributed to cited studies.

synthesis.inclusion: not_stated: narrative review with no stated search strategy, search dates, or inclusion criteria; 136 numbered references (pp. 21-38). The creativity evidence it cites (p. 15): refs 124 (Anderson, Shah, and Kreminski 2024) and 125 (Doshi and Hauser 2024) on LLM-assisted ideation and semantic similarity across participants, ref 126 (Dang et al. 2023) on deferring to model suggestions, ref 127 (Qin et al. 2025) on the timing of LLM use in ideation, and ref 128 (Kosmyna et al. 2025) on neural coupling in LLM-assisted essay writing.

company_involvement.description: None stated. Funding came from the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, grant A9550-23-1-046 (p. 20). The authors are at the University of Southern California (p. 1).

eligibility.reason: The screened arXiv v2 is a narrative review (p. 2, Abstract; p. 5, scope; main text pp. 3-17). It reports no random assignment of people to AI assistance, no participant sample analyzed, and no scoring of participant outputs of its own. The creative-ideation results on p. 15 are summaries of cited experiments [124, 125], not a reanalysis. All three core criteria are therefore not met; retain as synthesis context in the reference list only, with no estimates to extract. The cited experiments are separately represented in candidates.json as c001 and c006. Comparison with the journal version remains a provenance follow-up; this decision is based on the supplied preprint.

one_line_finding: Narrative review arguing that LLMs homogenize human language, perspective, and reasoning; on creativity it cites experiments (p. 15, refs [124, 125]) in which ChatGPT-assisted participants generated more, and more detailed and elaborated, ideas that were judged more semantically similar across participants, and it reports no new data or pooled numbers.
open_questions: The PDF on file is arXiv 2508.01491v2 (5 Jan 2026; PDF p. 1). The search record lists a journal version (Trends in Cognitive Sciences, DOI 10.1016/j.tics.2026.01.003), which has not been compared with the screened preprint. Its text, references, or supplementary material may differ. This is a version-provenance follow-up; no eligibility criterion is unresolved for the screened narrative review.
notes: Creativity passage (p. 15, Reasoning Diversity): 'participants who received assistance from LLMs (i.e., ChatGPT) generated a greater number of more detailed and elaborated ideas ... However, their outputs were also judged to be more semantically similar across participants [124, 125].' Creativity citations on p. 15: [124] Anderson, Shah, and Kreminski (2024, Creativity & Cognition), [125] Doshi and Hauser (2024, Science Advances), [126] Dang et al. (2023, CHI), [127] Qin et al. (2025, CHI), [128] Kosmyna et al. (2025, arXiv 2506.08872). Related citations on p. 13: [51] Jakesch et al. (2023, CHI) on co-writing with opinionated language models, and [105] Agarwal, Naaman, and Vashistha (2025, CHI), 'Ai suggestions homogenize writing toward western styles and diminish cultural nuances'. Cited works in the current candidates.json: [124] = c001, [125] = c006, [127] = c106, [105] = c026, [104] = c143, [19] = c118, [128] = c416, [51] = c799. The c001 record includes the cited Creativity & Cognition title as a title variant. No matching record was found for [126]. Reference identities were checked in the PDF: [19] p. 23; [51] p. 27; [104, 105] p. 34; [124] pp. 36-37; [125-128] p. 37. The document has no tables and one conceptual figure without data (Figure 1, p. 6). The review is not systematic, so k_studies and n_effect_sizes are null. The assignment unit and structure, the population, the AI role, and the task type are forced choices with no meaning for a review. The acknowledgment's sentence 'The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript' is a standard funder clause. The paper reports no data collection. Apart from the supplement code, the two raw forms differed only in wording or in extra detail (summary, label, version string, company description, inclusion, reason, finding, notes, open question). This form merges them. Finalization read the entire markdown conversion, including all back matter, and checked eligibility passages, version, page and reference counts, and retained bibliographic numbers against PDF text. No c023 challenge files were present, and reconciliation has no unresolved differences. The challenge-resolution counters are therefore zero. Finalizer clarifications scope supplement claims to the screened preprint and update the candidate cross-references; the reconciliation object is preserved unchanged.
